clue.text: Setter's speciality is highly dangerous

definitions.note: the definition is an adjective phrase standing for the noun: a place or situation that is highly dangerous

parts.note: the setter speaks of himself, so the setter's is my own: mine
one's speciality is one's field of expertise

explanation.surface: A crossword compiler boasts that his particular expertise is something perilous.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Setter's speciality' as 'my field': the setter's is MINE, a speciality is a FIELD.
explanation.definitionFit: A buried-explosives zone, or figuratively any situation full of hidden hazards, is highly dangerous to cross.

clue.text: The Way to the Stars?

parts.note: the title of a wartime film is read as a description of the galaxy, the starry Way across the night sky

explanation.surface: A film title, The Way to the Stars, offered as a quiz question.
explanation.walkthrough: The Way to the Stars is a 1945 British war film; here 'the Way' of stars is our galaxy, whose name has this adjective in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Our galaxy is called the Milky Way, so this adjective is what goes before Way among the stars.

clue.text: Brief communication not seen over the box

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: seen over means looked at the other way round, so the word for the box is read backwards

parts.note: the box is British slang for television, the telly or tele

explanation.surface: A short message went unnoticed beyond the television set.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seen over' turns TELE, a British slang word for the TV (the box), into ELET.
explanation.definitionFit: A short folded sheet for writing a quick note is a brief communication.

clue.text: Macbeth's intended victim abandons party to escape

indicators.note: abandons means the party's letters are dropped from the victim's name

parts.note: Fleance, Banquo's son, escapes the murderers Macbeth sends after him
the ANC is the African National Congress, a South African political party

explanation.surface: A Shakespearean character walks out on a political party in order to get away.
explanation.walkthrough: In Macbeth, Banquo's son FLEANCE is marked for murder but escapes; dropping ANC leaves FLE + E.
explanation.definitionFit: To flee is to run away from danger, which is to escape.

clue.text: 27 possibly loses head but keeps direction

indicators.note: loses head means the first letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: 27 across, a saint's day, is one example of a feast in the church calendar

explanation.surface: A holy day is decapitated yet stays on course.
explanation.walkthrough: A saint's day (27) is an example of a FEAST; 'loses head' removes the F.
explanation.definitionFit: East is one of the four compass points, each of which is a direction.

clue.text: Fed up with loving, though it could be leading one to court

definitions.text: it could be leading one to court

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: taken as written
amatory means relating to love, loving

explanation.surface: Someone sick of romance warns that it might end in a courtship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' is the reversal signal in this down clue. 'Court' suggests wooing after 'loving', but it is a court of law.
explanation.definitionFit: A defamatory remark is libellous or slanderous, and could land the speaker in a court of law.

clue.text: Female with dead expression, past her prime

indicators.note: expression here means the letters are pressed out into a new form, rearranged

explanation.surface: A woman with a lifeless face who is no longer young.
explanation.walkthrough: 'expression' is an unusual anagram signal: the letters are pressed out into a new shape, not a facial look.
explanation.definitionFit: Something faded has lost its brightness or vigour, as someone past her prime has.

clue.text: Warning — a man on board, somewhere on the ship

parts.note: fore is the golfer's shout of warning
a castle, or rook, is a chessman on the chessboard

explanation.surface: A caution is shouted as a sailor stands somewhere on deck.
explanation.walkthrough: FORE is the warning shouted on a golf course. 'a man on board' sounds like a sailor, but it is a chess piece.
explanation.definitionFit: The forecastle is the forward part of a ship, under or at the bow, so it is a location aboard.

clue.text: Like a damp squib, gone off in resentment

parts.note: a damp squib fails to go off, so it is a dud

indicators.note: off means gone wrong, so the letters of gone are rearranged

explanation.surface: A firework that fizzles out provokes a huff.
explanation.walkthrough: A squib is a small firework; a damp one is a DUD. 'off' reworks GONE into GEON.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in high dudgeon is to be indignant, so the word means a feeling of resentment.

clue.text: Hating to upset, Hughes gets in turmoil

indicators.note: upset means turned over, so the name is written backwards in this down light

parts.note: Ted Hughes was Poet Laureate

indicators.note: turmoil means disorder, so the letters of gets in are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone loathes causing distress as the poet falls into confusion.
explanation.walkthrough: TED (the poet Ted Hughes) is turned by 'upset' to DET; 'turmoil' rearranges GETS IN into ESTING. 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Detesting means loathing intensely, which is hating.

clue.text: Direct recourse to 11 before plastic

parts.note: 11 is cash (smackers); before credit cards, a traveller drew money directly on bank documents addressed to a foreign banker

explanation.surface: How people got hold of cash before credit cards.
explanation.walkthrough: 11 across is SMACKERS, slang for pounds; 'plastic' is credit cards.
explanation.definitionFit: These bank documents authorised the bearer to draw money abroad, the pre-card way of getting cash.

clue.text: See about a back door key

indicators.note: back means the whole assembled word is read in reverse
about means the see's name goes around the letter

parts.note: Ely is a cathedral city in Cambridgeshire, the seat of a bishop, a see

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to look round a rear entrance key.
explanation.walkthrough: ELY, a bishop's see, goes 'about' A to make ELAY; 'back' turns that into the answer. 'See' looks like a verb but is a diocese.
explanation.definitionFit: Yale is a brand of cylinder lock, and the name is used for the key that opens such a door.

clue.text: What most of the fish aboard may fetch

annotationWithheld.why: What most of the fish aboard may fetch (8): MACKER(el) inside SS, but 'aboard' must both supply SS (on a steamship) and signal the insertion, one word doing two jobs
annotationWithheld.clue: What most of the fish aboard may fetch

clue.text: Cul-de-sacs have a narrow escape

parts.note: in Britain a close is a dead-end residential street, a cul-de-sac
taken as written

explanation.surface: Dead-end streets come with a tight getaway.
explanation.walkthrough: A close is a common British name for a short dead-end street.
explanation.definitionFit: A close shave is an idiom for a lucky near miss, a narrow escape from danger.

clue.text: Real things unlikely to be from outer space

definitions.text: Real things unlikely to be from outer space

indicators.note: unlikely means not as they appear, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Genuine objects are improbably extraterrestrial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unlikely' reworks REAL THINGS; the whole clue also describes the answer: real beings who are not aliens.
explanation.definitionFit: Inhabitants of our planet are, by definition, not visitors from outer space.

clue.text: Tell a pint — poured out it's sparkling

indicators.note: poured out suggests liquid spilling and splashing, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Ordering a pint at the bar, someone notes it fizzes once poured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poured out' rearranges TELL A PINT; 'it's' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Pétillant is a wine term, borrowed from French, for lightly sparkling.

clue.text: One's used to picking up the bill

definitions.text: One's used to picking up the bill

parts.words: One's used to picking up the bill
parts.note: the Bill is British slang for the police; the vehicle that ferries officers about picks them up

explanation.surface: Someone who habitually pays for everyone's dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Bill' (Old Bill) is British slang for the police, not a restaurant tab.
explanation.definitionFit: A patrol vehicle carries officers, the Bill in British slang, about their duties.

clue.text: Scene of bush fire is in a turmoil

indicators.note: turmoil means disorder, so the letters of is in a are jumbled

explanation.surface: A wildfire breaks out amid chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turmoil' rearranges IS IN A. The 'bush fire' is the Biblical burning bush, not an Australian wildfire.
explanation.definitionFit: Moses saw the burning bush on Mount Sinai, according to Exodus, so the place is its scene.

clue.text: Roger embraced by girl — like a monkey

definitions.note: an adjective phrase standing for a noun: a creature that resembles a monkey

indicators.note: embraced by means the letter is held inside the girl's name

parts.note: Lois is a girl's name
in radio procedure roger stands for the letter R, received

explanation.surface: A man is hugged by a young woman who behaves like an ape.
explanation.walkthrough: Roger is the radio alphabet's old word for R; it goes inside LOIS.
explanation.definitionFit: The loris is a small nocturnal primate of Asia, related to monkeys and resembling one.

clue.text: Endeavour by soldiers to show compunction

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, a corps of soldiers
Endeavour is the first name of Inspector Morse, the TV detective

explanation.surface: An effort by the army demonstrates guilt.
explanation.walkthrough: Inspector Morse, the British TV detective, has the rarely used first name Endeavour. 'by' puts RE beside him.
explanation.definitionFit: Compunction is a pang of guilt or regret, the same feeling as remorse.

clue.text: Article about Brook is highly emotive

indicators.note: about means the article's word surrounds the brook's

parts.note: an article is a thing, an object
a rill is a small stream, a brook

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece on a man called Brook stirs strong feelings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' suggests THE or A but is THING, an object; 'Brook' looks like a surname but is a stream.
explanation.definitionFit: Something thrilling excites strong feelings, so it is highly emotive.

clue.text: One member misled by not being told

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
an MP is a Member of Parliament
misled here means told untruths, which is lied

explanation.surface: A politician deceived people by keeping them in the dark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' is a link; the answer is suggested rather than stated.
explanation.definitionFit: Something implied is suggested without being said outright, so it is conveyed by not being told.

clue.text: Kingsley wearing old king's garment?

indicators.note: wearing means one name is clothed by the other, so the novelist sits inside the king

parts.note: Old King Cole is the merry old soul of the nursery rhyme
Kingsley Amis was an English novelist

explanation.surface: A novelist dons the garment of a nursery-rhyme monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: Old King Cole is the merry old soul of a nursery rhyme; 'wearing' has the king clothed around the novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: A camisole is a light sleeveless undergarment for the upper body, a type of garment.

clue.text: Hits back in altercation

indicators.note: back means the word is read the other way

parts.note: taps are light hits

explanation.surface: Someone strikes back during a quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns TAPS round; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A spat is a short petty quarrel, a minor altercation.

clue.text: Score went out, all substituted, score remained

indicators.note: out means the word went is taken out of the number
substituted means the letters of all are put in where those were

parts.note: a score is twenty
the clue's own letters, taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A match report: one side went out, everyone was replaced, and the score stood.
explanation.walkthrough: Score is TWENTY; take WENT out and put ALL in: T + ALL + Y. 'remained' is a link saying what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: A tally is a running count, such as the score in a game.

clue.text: One youngster set up as an artist

indicators.note: in a down clue, set up means the pieces are raised, read from bottom to top

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
a lad is a youngster

explanation.surface: A young person sets up as a painter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set up' reverses I + LAD in this down light. 'as' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Salvador Dalí was a Spanish surrealist painter, so he is an example of an artist.

clue.text: Attend for police duty

definitions.meaning: to attend somewhere is to ... it, the two words run together
a police officer's ... is the route patrolled on duty

explanation.surface: Turning up for a shift with the police.
explanation.walkthrough: The first definition splits as BE AT.
explanation.definitionFit: A constable's beat is the area patrolled, and to attend is to be at, written as one word.

clue.text: Fabrication of famous last words?

parts.note: fabrication is cloth, and famous last words come at the end, when the drape comes down on a show

explanation.surface: A suggestion that famous dying utterances are made up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fabrication' means lies on the surface but cloth here; 'curtains' means the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Fabric for drapes is literally this, and 'curtains' is slang for the end, when last words are said.

clue.text: Steward concerned with a girl

parts.note: re means concerning, with regard to
Eve is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A manager takes an interest in a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A reeve was a medieval steward or manager of an estate, an official in charge.

clue.text: All goes before it at the start of November

definitions.text: All goes before it at the start of November

parts.words: All goes before it at the start of November
parts.note: the festival on 1 November is named with the word All in front of these two words

explanation.surface: Something that everyone precedes at the beginning of November.
explanation.walkthrough: All Saints' Day falls on 1 November; 'All' comes before the answer in its full name.
explanation.definitionFit: A church feast honouring holy figures; with All in front it names the 1 November festival.
